body:
Reduce injury risks before shaking begins

Because the precise occurrence of an earthquake cannot be reliably predicted, earthquake preparedness must be completed in advance. Households, schools and workplaces should identify safer locations, practice basic protective actions and make plans for reconnecting with family members after an event.

Useful precautions include securing tall cupboards and heavy shelves, placing heavy objects on lower shelves, keeping exits accessible and ensuring that household members know how to obtain verified information. The structure of a building and its heavy fixtures should be inspected by qualified professionals where there is reason to doubt their safety.

What to do during an earthquake

For a person who is inside a building when shaking begins, the standard protective action is Drop, Cover and Hold On: drop to hands and knees, cover the head and neck and shelter beneath sturdy furniture if it is close enough, and hold on until shaking stops. If sturdy furniture is not available, move as little as possible and protect the head and neck away from windows and objects that may fall.

Do not rush down stairs or run outside while the ground is shaking. Do not use elevators. Ordinary doorways are not automatically safer than other indoor locations.

If already outdoors, move to a clear area away from buildings, trees, poles and overhead power lines, and stay there until shaking ends. If travelling in a vehicle, the driver should stop in a suitable clear location away from structures and power lines and remain stopped until the shaking ends.

After shaking stops

Aftershocks are additional earthquakes that follow a larger event and can further damage weakened structures. People should remain alert, avoid visibly damaged buildings and follow official instructions about evacuation or re-entry. Injured people may require medical assistance, while damaged electrical lines, possible gas leaks, broken glass and unstable walls present secondary dangers.

Use safe drinking water and reliable information. Do not enter damaged buildings simply to collect belongings until the location has been declared safe. Where an earthquake occurs near the coast, a strong or prolonged shock may also be a natural warning of a tsunami; once shaking stops, people in an exposed coastal area should move promptly to higher ground or inland.

The 26 January 2001 Gujarat earthquake

On 26 January 2001, a major earthquake struck the Kutch region of Gujarat, severely affecting Bhuj and surrounding settlements. Damage to buildings, roads, utilities and public facilities demonstrated that earthquake losses are shaped not only by the natural event but also by construction quality and the capacity for organised relief and recovery.

The Government of Gujarat established the Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority (GSDMA) as a registered society on 8 February 2001 to support rehabilitation, reconstruction, preparedness and mitigation. The Gujarat State Disaster Management Act, 2003 came into force on 13 May 2003, and GSDMA became a statutory authority with effect from 1 September 2003.

Gujarat's reconstruction experience illustrates the importance of safer housing, restoration of essential services, community involvement and long-term disaster-risk reduction. Recovery involves more than clearing debris. Families may need temporary shelter, restored livelihoods, functioning schools and health facilities, support for rebuilding and measures that reduce future structural vulnerability.

Institutional responsibilities

The National Centre for Seismology (NCS), under the Ministry of Earth Sciences, monitors earthquake activity and reports recorded events. State and district authorities coordinate public preparedness, relief and recovery. Professional rescue teams undertake specialised operations, while citizens contribute by following safety instructions, assisting vulnerable neighbours when safe and avoiding rumours.

Prelims focus

  • During indoor shaking: Drop, Cover and Hold On.
  • Aftershocks can further damage already weakened buildings.
  • The major Kutch earthquake occurred on 26 January 2001.
  • GSDMA was initially established on 8 February 2001.
  • The Gujarat State Disaster Management Act, 2003, came into force on 13 May 2003.
  • Trap: Earthquake response begins with protection during shaking, not running outside immediately.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, Chapter 3, Our Changing Earth, printed pp. 13–14, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 15, Some Natural Phenomena, printed pp. 191–195, 2018–19 printing; National Centre for Seismology, public earthquake safety guidance and seismic monitoring information; Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, About Us and Gujarat State Disaster Management Act, 2003, historical and statutory-status sections; Ministry of Earth Sciences, Parliament Question: Seismograph Network, 1 April 2026. Official sources consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Earthquake Preparedness, Public Safety and Gujarat's Recovery Experience

body:
What is a tsunami?

A tsunami is a series of long ocean waves caused by the sudden displacement of a large volume of water. It is most commonly generated by a major earthquake beneath or near the sea that significantly moves the seafloor.

Tsunamis may also result from submarine landslides and volcanic activity. The essential physical condition is rapid displacement of water, not simply the occurrence of an earthquake. An earthquake that does not sufficiently displace the water column may produce little or no tsunami.

The word tsunami is associated with the Japanese term for a harbour wave. Despite its name, a tsunami is not a normal astronomical tide. Ordinary tides arise mainly from the gravitational effects of the Moon and the Sun. Tsunamis are also different from the short wind-generated waves commonly seen on beaches.

Generation at an undersea fault

At some convergent plate boundaries, one tectonic plate moves beneath another. This is called a subduction zone. If a large earthquake abruptly raises or lowers part of the seafloor, the overlying water is displaced. Gravity then acts to restore the water surface, generating waves that travel away from the disturbance.

A major undersea earthquake is therefore an important possible tsunami source, but neither a particular magnitude alone nor the location beneath the ocean guarantees that a destructive tsunami will occur. The type and extent of seafloor movement matter.

Why a tsunami changes near the coast

In deep water, a tsunami has a very long wavelength and may travel across an ocean basin at high speed while producing only a small change in surface height. Ships in deep water may not notice its passage.

As the wave enters shallower coastal water, it slows and its wavelength shortens. Its height and the strength of its currents may increase. This process is called shoaling. Depending on local conditions, a tsunami may arrive as a rapidly rising flood, a turbulent surge or a breaking wave.

Inundation and run-up

Inundation is the flooding of normally dry land by tsunami water. Run-up is the maximum vertical elevation reached by tsunami water above a specified reference sea level at the coast. These terms describe different aspects of tsunami impact: one concerns the flooding of land, and the other concerns the height to which the water reaches.

The resulting danger extends beyond the visible wave. Powerful inflowing and outgoing currents can sweep away people, vehicles and debris. Harbours, estuaries, river mouths, low-lying settlements and coastal roads may be particularly exposed. Waves can enter some rivers and channels connected to the sea.

One tsunami can produce many dangerous arrivals

A tsunami usually consists of a series of waves, not a single wave. Its first arrival may not be its highest or most destructive. Waves and dangerous currents can continue for hours. Sudden withdrawal of seawater before an incoming wave is a possible warning sign, but it does not occur in every tsunami.

The 26 December 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, generated by a major undersea earthquake near the Sunda-Andaman region, affected several Indian Ocean countries and caused major destruction along parts of India's eastern coast and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. It demonstrated how one distant geological event could create widespread coastal impacts.

Prelims focus

  • Rapid displacement of seawater is the essential physical cause of a tsunami.
  • Major submarine earthquakes, landslides and volcanic activity can generate tsunamis.
  • Tsunami waves usually slow and may grow higher as they enter shallow water.
  • Inundation means flooding of normally dry land; run-up refers to the vertical height reached.
  • The major Indian Ocean tsunami occurred on 26 December 2004.
  • Trap: The first tsunami wave is not necessarily the largest.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 15, Some Natural Phenomena, printed pp. 191–192, 2018–19 printing; National Disaster Management Authority, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Tsunamis, August 2010, Chapter 1; National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, Tsunamis and Tsunami Inundation, sections on generation, propagation, run-up and multiple waves; U.S. Geological Survey, Life of a Tsunami, sections on coastal impact and persistence. Online sources consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Seafloor movement generates long, low, fast tsunami waves that slow and may grow higher in shallow water, flooding coastal land.
pictures.caption: A tsunami can be difficult to notice in deep water but become destructive as it reaches a shallow coast.

title: How Tsunamis Form, Travel and Inundate Coastal Areas

body:
Warning begins after a potential tsunami-generating event

A tsunami-warning system cannot normally predict the exact time of the undersea earthquake that will generate a tsunami. Instead, it rapidly detects the triggering earthquake, assesses whether a tsunami may have formed, checks ocean observations and issues advisories to authorities and exposed communities.

India's Indian Tsunami Early Warning System is operated through the Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS) at Hyderabad, under the Ministry of Earth Sciences. The fully operational 24-hour warning service was established in October 2007, following the experience of the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami.

Main components of the system

  • Seismic monitoring: Detects and locates an earthquake and estimates whether it could generate a tsunami.
  • Deep-ocean bottom-pressure recorders: Detect changes associated with tsunami waves passing through deep water.
  • Tide gauges: Observe changes in sea level at coastal and island stations.
  • Numerical models: Estimate possible wave travel times, coastal effects and areas at risk.
  • Warning communication: Sends advisories to relevant government agencies and other recipients so that communities can receive timely instructions.

A large submarine earthquake may justify an initial advisory before a tsunami is fully confirmed by sea-level instruments. Later observations help update the assessment. This is why warnings can change as new information becomes available.

Understanding tsunami advisories

The Indian system distinguishes the expected threat and the corresponding public action. These labels must be understood in the context of the advisory issued for the affected coastal zone.

Threat statusGeneral meaningPublic implication
WarningPotentially dangerous tsunami inundationMove inland or towards higher ground as advised
AlertDangerous conditions may affect coastal marine areasAvoid beaches and low-lying coastal areas
WatchThreat requires continued monitoringStay informed and prepare to act if instructions change
Threat passedMonitoring indicates that the assessed threat has passedReturn only when local authorities give the all-clear

The all-clear decision for the public is made by the relevant local authorities. A technical bulletin alone does not justify entering an unsafe shore or harbour.

Why natural warnings still matter

A tsunami generated close to a coast may arrive before an official warning has reached everyone. A person who experiences strong or prolonged earthquake shaking near the sea, observes an unusual sudden rise or withdrawal of seawater, or hears an unusual roaring sound from the sea should recognise a possible natural warning and move away from the exposed coast without waiting for a formal message.

Gujarat's tsunami risk

Gujarat's long coastline faces the Arabian Sea. Although tsunamis are much less frequent than ordinary coastal waves or cyclone-related coastal flooding, the possibility cannot be dismissed.

The Gujarat State Disaster Management Plan identifies the Makran Subduction Zone, southwest of Karachi in the Arabian Sea, as a possible source of major submarine earthquakes capable of producing a tsunami affecting Gujarat. It is therefore incorrect to assume that only India's eastern coastline can experience tsunami risk.

Low-lying coastal settlements, fishing harbours, ports and estuaries require particular attention in coastal-risk planning. Local geography influences whether water is concentrated, how far it travels inland and which evacuation routes remain usable.

Prelims focus

  • INCOIS operates India's tsunami early-warning service from Hyderabad.
  • The fully operational Indian Tsunami Early Warning System dates from October 2007.
  • Seismic stations detect earthquakes; deep-ocean sensors and tide gauges help monitor tsunami waves.
  • A tsunami Warning calls for movement towards higher ground or inland.
  • Makran Subduction Zone is a relevant Arabian Sea tsunami source for Gujarat.
  • Trap: An official tsunami warning may arrive too late for some near-source coastal communities.

[Sources: Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services, Indian Tsunami Early Warning System, About the System and Standard Operating Procedure, sections on monitoring components, operational history and threat-status actions; Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Gujarat State Disaster Management Plan 2020–21, Volume 2, Chapter 3, Action Plan for Tsunami, Section 3.1, printed p. 31; National Disaster Management Authority, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Tsunamis, August 2010, chapters on warning and preparedness. Official sources consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: India's tsunami warning process links earthquake detection, ocean observations, hazard assessment and public communication.

title: Tsunami Early Warning in India and Gujarat's Coastal Exposure

body:
Evacuation is the principal immediate life-saving measure

Once a dangerous tsunami is expected or natural warning signs are noticed, people in the threatened coastal area should move quickly to higher ground or farther inland, following recognised evacuation routes and instructions where these are available. The objective is to get beyond the likely inundation area before the waves arrive.

If strong earthquake shaking occurs first, people should protect themselves from falling objects during the shaking. As soon as movement becomes safe, they should leave the exposed coastal zone. Do not go towards the beach to watch the sea or collect fish from an unexpectedly exposed seabed.

People should not return merely because the first wave has receded. Successive waves and strong currents may continue for many hours. The safe time to return depends on conditions and instructions from local authorities.

Reducing exposure before a tsunami

Effective planning requires identifying low-lying coastal areas, mapping possible inundation, keeping evacuation routes accessible and ensuring that people understand how to reach safer locations. Schools, fishing communities, tourist areas and settlements with limited transport need practical evacuation arrangements.

Preparedness must include people who may need additional assistance, including children, older persons and persons with disabilities. Public warnings are useful only when they reach people in time and are followed by feasible protective actions.

Natural coastal ecosystems as protective buffers

Coastal ecosystems can help reduce some effects of incoming water and waves. Their contribution depends on the characteristics of the hazard, the width and condition of the ecosystem and the shape of the coast.

  • Mangroves: Roots and vegetation can help stabilise coastal sediments, reduce erosion and slow or dissipate some water movement under suitable conditions.
  • Sand dunes: Intact dunes can act as elevated natural barriers against some coastal flooding and erosion.
  • Coastal vegetation: Shelterbelts and other appropriate vegetation can contribute to protection and sediment stability.
  • Coral reefs: Healthy reefs can dissipate some incoming wave energy and reduce erosion in suitable coastal environments.

Natural buffers are not substitutes for evacuation. A sufficiently powerful tsunami can cross or damage mangroves, dunes, reefs and other natural barriers. Coastal protection should combine ecosystem conservation with hazard-aware land use, warning communication and evacuation planning.

Recovery after tsunami inundation

Tsunami recovery may involve damage caused by seawater, deposited sediments, floating debris and strong currents. Houses, roads, fishing vessels, landing facilities, water supplies and agricultural land may be affected.

Saltwater contamination can damage drinking-water sources and reduce the immediate agricultural usefulness of some soils. Fishing households may lose boats, nets, engines and market access even when their homes remain standing.

Recovery priorities therefore include safe shelter, drinking water, sanitation, repair of essential services and restoration of livelihoods. Rebuilding should account for coastal exposure rather than automatically reconstructing every damaged structure at the same vulnerable site. Conserving natural ecosystems and improving evacuation facilities can reduce future risk.

Prelims focus

  • Natural tsunami warnings include strong or long coastal earthquake shaking and unusual sea-level change.
  • Evacuation should be towards higher ground or inland.
  • The first tsunami wave may not be the largest.
  • Mangroves and dunes can provide partial natural protection.
  • Tsunami recovery may require restoring fisheries and addressing saltwater contamination.
  • Trap: Visible withdrawal of seawater is a possible danger signal, not an opportunity to approach the shore.

[Sources: National Disaster Management Authority, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Tsunamis, August 2010, chapters on preparedness, coastal land use and ecosystem-based protection; National Disaster Management Plan, 2016, tsunami-related non-structural mitigation and bio-shield measures; National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, Tsunamis, sections on natural warnings and safe evacuation; Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services, tsunami advisory Standard Operating Procedure, section on all-clear determination. Official sources consulted 2 November 2026.]
